extracted.intended_audience: architects, designers, art students, and educated readers interested in architectural ornament, materials, and figurative representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for judging and producing architectural ornament, material choices (glass, iron, stone), and modes of representing natural elements (especially water). Intended as prescriptive/critical rules for architects, sculptors, and designers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of ornament conditional on quality and stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: "You cannot have too much ornament, if it be good: but if you are too indolent to arrange it, or too dull to take advantage of it, assuredly you are better without it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantity is acceptable provided the ornament is good and the owner/user is willing and able to arrange, care for, and profit by it. Poorly managed or poorly understood ornament becomes a detriment; do not add ornament that will be neglected or confuse the user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of manual labour as a chief source of value in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: "The appearance of labour, that is to say, the evidence of the past industry of man, is always, in the abstract, intensely delightful..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delight arises from seeing human industry embodied in work. This evidence is valuable except where the labour signifies weakness (inefficiency), folly (labour expended on unworthy ends), or failure (labour without accomplishment). Where labour replaces skill and thought it becomes a positive evil; conversely, the utter absence of labour in human work destroys value. Machine-made ornament is condemned: "machine ornaments are no ornaments at all." Practical experience (e.g., attempting a manual trade) is recommended to appreciate the value of human labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let labour substitute for thought and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whenever labour replaces what was better than labour, that is to say, skill and thought... then it is positive evil."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament that exists only as laborious surface-work without underlying intelligent design or technical skill dishonors the industry invested. Prioritise thought and technical skill over mere labour-intensive decoration. Avoid labour that negates or supplants more valuable intellectual or technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two means of delight in art: colour and form; hierarchy of colour
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two means of delight in all productions of art — color and form."  "The best and noblest coloring possible to art is that attained by the touch of the human hand on an opaque surface... The next best is the scientific disposition of the natural colors of stones... The delight which we receive from glass painting is one altogether inferior..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting materials and treatments, consider (1) painted/hand-applied colour on opaque surfaces as the noblest; (2) natural colours of stones as the next best for architecture; (3) stained or painted glass and enamel provide vivid colors but are inferior and degrade if overused. Colour may be used on opaque or transparent media, but preference in architecture should favour opaque materials and natural stone colouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must be expressed on opaque, lustreless matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Form is only expressible, in its perfection, on opaque bodies, without lustre. This law is imperative, universal, irrevocable. No perfect or refined form can be expressed except in opaque and lustreless matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For achieving refined, noble forms in architecture and sculpture, choose opaque, non-lustrous materials (stone, fine matte metal/bronze, treated iron). Highly lustrous or transparent materials (glass, polished metals, burnished surfaces) obscure or prevent the perception of refined form; exceptions only where iron/enamel can be made lustreless and fine in texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a work of art proportional to expressed humanity: thought, skill, industry
rubrics_metrics.description: "And the value of every work of art is exactly in the ratio of the quantity of humanity which has been put into it, and legibly expressed upon it for ever: — First, of thought and moral purpose; Secondly, of technical skill; Thirdly, of bodily industry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging artwork or architectural ornament, weigh contributions in the order: intellectual/moral purpose, technical skill, and bodily labour. The clearer and more legible the human intention and mind in the work, the greater its value. Multiplicability (casts, engravings) does not necessarily diminish intrinsic worth if fidelity to the original's humanity is retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and appropriate uses of glass and iron in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is thought by many that we shall forthwith have great part of our architecture in glass and iron... It may be told in a few words how far this is possible; how far eternally impossible... The most vivid conditions of color attainable by human art are those of works in glass... The delight which we receive from glass painting is one altogether inferior... No noble architecture can ever, therefore, be produced in transparent or lustrous glass or enamel. Iron is, however, opaque; and both it and opaque enamel may, perhaps, be rendered quite lustreless; and, therefore, fit to receive noble form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat glass as limited: its vivid colour is useful in moderation (stained-glass palaces as novelty) but cannot replace the capacity of opaque materials to express noble form. Iron could be acceptable terrain for noble architecture only if rendered opaque and lustreless and given fine texture; avoid substituting sheer industrial productivity or novelty of material for deep thought and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of representing natural elements (water): natural, conventional, figurative, symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: natural representation = as just and perfect an imitation of nature as technical means allow; conventional = an accepted inadequate imitation or substitute sign; figurative = impersonation (organic form endowed with will); symbolic = sensible sign or equivalent not personified. "Though the conventionally imitative, the figurative, and the symbolic, are three distinct kinds of representation, they are constantly combined in one composition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mode appropriate to purpose and cultural language. Use naturalistic depiction when technical means and desire for realism require it; use conventional signs (zigzag lines, wave mouldings, meander) as economical, culturally-legible shorthand; use figurative personification when imbuing natural forces with human attributes; use symbols when a visible sign suffices without personification. Be aware these modes are commonly combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established conventional motifs (wave moulding, meander) as hieroglyphic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: "Two conventional imitations, the wave moulding and the meander, are well known... In the wave moulding we have a conventional representation of the small crisping waves... their regular succession... are generalised in this moulding... it is this eternity of recurrence which the early artist has expressed in this hieroglyphic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ motifs like the wave moulding and the meander when you wish to generalise recurring natural phenomena or convey enduring, cyclical character (e.g., the sea). Such motifs function as artistic 'hieroglyphs' — stylised, repeatable signs that communicate idea/feeling rather than exact visual fidelity. Combine these with figurative or symbolic elements for richer compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different cultural solutions for representing water (Egyptian, Assyrian, Greek examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Egyptian: water by parallel zigzag lines and reduced pictographs; Assyrian: wavy lines terminating in curls/volutes suggesting deep rapid current; Greek: a variety including wave mouldings, meander, sculptured overlapping-tile waves and many aquatic deities/figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing water, consider cultural conventions and the intended expressive effect: use Egyptian-like zigzag shorthand for schematic or symbolic depiction; Assyrian wavy volutes for dynamic currents; Greek combinations (conventional motifs + figurative deities) when richness, typology, and mythic association are desired. Study historical precedents to select the mode that best fits the compositional and communicative aim.
